title: Miriam's timbrel (Exodus 15:20–21)
hookLine: the prophetess takes a drum and leads the women in dance

lines: A DRUM IS HARD TO PACK.
NO TIME FOR THE BREAD TO RISE.
cards: A drum is an awkward thing to pack. It's round, it's bulky, and it doesn't feed anybody. The Israelites left Egypt so fast the bread didn't have time to rise.
And yet, on the far shore, with the water closed and the people safe, one woman reaches into her bag and pulls out a drum. Then another woman does. And another.

teach.b: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances."
Three things in one line. First, the title: the Torah itself calls Miriam a prophetess. Why the sister of Aaron, and not of Moses?
The Talmud answers with a story: she prophesied when she was only Aaron's sister, before Moses was born, that her mother would have a son who would save the people.
Tradition says she's the girl who watched the basket on the Nile. Now she's leading the women in dance. Second, the drum.

teach.h: A HAND DRUM, PACKED IN EGYPT.
teach.b: A timbrel is a hand drum, skin stretched over a frame, held up and struck with the palm. The midrash asks: where did these women get drums, in the desert, after leaving in such a rush?

The answer, which Rashi passes on: they were so sure God would do wonders for them that they packed their drums in Egypt. They carried the celebration before there was anything to celebrate. Third, the song.

Miriam sings one line back to the women, "Sing ye to the LORD, for He is highly exalted", nearly the line Moses opened with. Moses sings the long song; Miriam gets everyone dancing. Both belong to the story.
Some Jewish women today point to this verse when they sing, drum and lead in their own communities.

teach.h: HOPE YOU PUT IN YOUR BAG.
teach.b: And the lesson inside it is quiet: hope isn't only a feeling.

teach.h: AND ALL THE WOMEN WENT OUT AFTER HER.
teach.b: Sometimes it's a thing you put in your bag.

how: Miriam's song is read in synagogue with the Song of the Sea each year, and in many communities women mark it by singing and drumming together, some on the seventh day of Passover.

o: a hand drum the women packed before leaving Egypt
a ram's horn blown to call the people together
a harp Miriam played in Pharaoh's palace

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: they packed the drums in Egypt

s: the Torah calls Miriam a prophetess
"Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron."
Miriam sang a long song of her own
she sang one line back to the women, nearly the line Moses opened with.
the Torah says where the drums came from
it doesn't. the midrash, quoted by Rashi, says the women packed them in Egypt out of trust.

games.q: you're one of the women, packing to leave Egypt tonight. there's no time and almost no room. what goes in the bag?
o: nothing: you'll leave it all behind.
games.why: the midrash says the women packed their drums, so sure of wonders that they carried the celebration before it came.

practice: Move for one minute. If you can stand, stand; if you can't, your hands and shoulders will do: tap a rhythm on your leg or the table like a hand drum, sway, nod, with nobody watching and nobody grading.
Then be still for a minute, and notice your heartbeat, the drum you always carry.

wordCard.voice: Miriam's timbrel. A hand drum, carried out of Egypt by women who were sure they'd need it, and played on the far shore of the sea.

orig.note: Hebrew: a hand drum, the timbrel Miriam played. the same word appears in the Psalms' lists of instruments.

carryVoice: Your line: bring the drum. Hope can be packed before the good news comes. That's day ninety-one.
